questions.stem:
(a) Name the two main components of a forest ecosystem and give two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) Explain four functions (services) that forest ecosystems perform for the environment. [8 marks]
(c) Describe how energy flows through a forest food chain, using a named example. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Biotic (living) components, e.g. trees, shrubs, herbs, animals, fungi, bacteria (1 mark for component, 2 for two examples)
3 marks: (a) Abiotic (non-living) components, e.g. soil, water, air, light, temperature, rainfall (1 mark for component, 2 for two examples)
8 marks: (b) Any four explained, 2 marks each: carbon sequestration/climate regulation; protection of soil from erosion; watershed protection/regulation of water flow; nutrient cycling; habitat for wildlife/biodiversity conservation; oxygen production; windbreak; moderation of local temperature and humidity
2 marks: (c) Green plants trap sunlight energy by photosynthesis and store it in food
2 marks: (c) Named chain, e.g. leaves -> grasshopper -> lizard -> hawk / leaves -> antelope -> leopard; energy passes from one trophic level to the next by feeding
2 marks: (c) At each level energy is lost as heat in respiration and in wastes, so less energy reaches higher levels; flow is one-way; dead matter energy goes to decomposers
questions.explanation: Forest ecosystems have biotic (trees, animals, decomposers) and abiotic (soil, water, light) components. They store carbon, protect soil and watersheds, recycle nutrients, harbour biodiversity and moderate climate. Energy enters through photosynthesis and passes along chains such as leaves -> antelope -> leopard, with losses as heat at each level.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a national park and a game reserve. [4 marks]
(b) Name two national parks in Nigeria and the state in which each is located. [4 marks]
(c) Explain four practices used in managing wildlife in a protected area. [8 marks]
(d) State four reasons why some wildlife species have become endangered in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) National park: area protected by the federal government for conservation of wildlife and habitats, education and tourism; hunting is not allowed
2 marks: (a) Game reserve: area set aside (often by state government) mainly to protect game animals; controlled/licensed hunting may be allowed
4 marks: (b) Any two correctly located, 2 marks each: Kainji Lake (Niger/Kwara); Old Oyo (Oyo); Cross River (Cross River); Gashaka-Gumti (Taraba/Adamawa); Chad Basin (Borno/Yobe); Kamuku (Kaduna); Okomu (Edo)
8 marks: (c) Any four explained, 2 marks each: anti-poaching patrols by rangers; habitat management (controlled burning, water provision); closed seasons and hunting licences; population census/monitoring; translocation and restocking; control of diseases; fencing/buffer zones; community education and involvement; captive breeding
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: habitat destruction/deforestation; poaching/over-hunting for bushmeat; illegal wildlife trade; bush burning; farming and grazing encroachment; pollution; weak law enforcement
questions.explanation: National parks are federal protected areas where hunting is banned; game reserves protect game and may allow licensed hunting. Examples include Kainji Lake, Old Oyo, Cross River, Gashaka-Gumti and Okomu. Management uses ranger patrols, habitat management, closed seasons, census, restocking and community education. Species decline through habitat loss, poaching, trade and burning.

questions.stem:
(a) Define deforestation. [2 marks]
(b) Explain five causes of deforestation in Nigeria. [10 marks]
(c) State four effects of deforestation on the environment. [4 marks]
(d) Suggest four measures to reduce deforestation. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The clearing or removal of forest cover, permanently converting forest land to non-forest uses
10 marks: (b) Any five explained, 2 marks each: shifting cultivation and farmland expansion; logging for timber (often illegal); fuelwood and charcoal production; urbanisation and road/infrastructure construction; bush burning; overgrazing; mining and oil exploration; population pressure
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: soil erosion; loss of biodiversity and wildlife habitat; desertification; climate change/increased CO2; reduced rainfall; flooding and siltation of rivers; loss of forest products and income
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: afforestation and reforestation; enforcement of forest laws; use of alternative energy (gas, solar) instead of fuelwood; agroforestry/taungya; public education; controlled logging/sustainable management; community forestry
questions.explanation: Deforestation is permanent removal of forest. It is driven by farming, logging, fuelwood and charcoal, urbanisation, bush burning, grazing and mining. It causes erosion, biodiversity loss, desertification, climate change and flooding. Remedies include planting trees, enforcing laws, alternative energy, agroforestry and education.

questions.stem:
A forestry department plans to establish a 2-hectare Gmelina arborea plantation at a spacing of 2.5 m x 2.5 m. An extra 10% of seedlings is needed for beating up (replacing dead seedlings). Each seedling costs N150. Land clearing costs N60 000 per hectare, and planting labour costs N20 per seedling planted (including those used for beating up).
(a) Calculate the number of seedlings needed per hectare at the given spacing. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total number of seedlings needed for 2 hectares, including beating up. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate (i) the cost of seedlings; (ii) the cost of land clearing; (iii) the cost of planting labour; (iv) the total establishment cost. [8 marks]
(d) What is beating up and why is it necessary? [3 marks]
(e) State four tending operations to be carried out after planting. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) 10 000 / (2.5 x 2.5) = 10 000 / 6.25 = 1600 seedlings per hectare
1 mark: (b) For 2 ha: 1600 x 2 = 3200
2 marks: (b) Beating up: 10% of 3200 = 320; total = 3520 seedlings
2 marks: (c)(i) 3520 x N150 = N528 000
2 marks: (c)(ii) 2 x N60 000 = N120 000
2 marks: (c)(iii) 3520 x N20 = N70 400
2 marks: (c)(iv) 528 000 + 120 000 + 70 400 = N718 400
1 mark: (d) Replacing seedlings that have died after planting
2 marks: (d) To maintain the planned stocking/spacing so that the land is fully used and yield is not reduced
4 marks: (e) Any four, 1 mark each: weeding; pruning; thinning; fire protection (firebreaks); fertiliser application; pest and disease control; climber cutting
questions.explanation: At 2.5 m x 2.5 m there are 1600 seedlings per hectare, 3200 for 2 ha, plus 320 for beating up = 3520. Costs: seedlings N528 000, clearing N120 000, labour N70 400, total N718 400. Beating up replaces dead seedlings to maintain stocking. Tending includes weeding, pruning, thinning, fire protection and pest control.

questions.stem:
(a) What is marketing of forest products? [2 marks]
(b) Name three agencies or channels involved in marketing forest products in Nigeria. [3 marks]
(c) Explain five functions of marketing agencies for forest products. [10 marks]
(d) State five problems of marketing forest products in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) All the activities involved in moving forest products from the forest (producer) to the final consumer, including buying, assembling, processing, transporting, storing and selling
3 marks: (b) Any three, 1 mark each: sawmillers/timber merchants; timber contractors/concessionaires; state forestry departments/forestry commissions; co-operatives of NTFP collectors; wholesalers and retailers; exporters; furniture makers
10 marks: (c) Any five explained, 2 marks each: assembling/buying from producers; transportation to markets; storage and seasoning; processing (sawing, drying); grading and standardisation; financing/credit to producers; market information; advertising/promotion; distribution to consumers; risk bearing
5 marks: (d) Any five, 1 mark each: poor roads/high transport cost; bulky and heavy products; lack of storage/processing facilities; price fluctuations; illegal logging/undercutting; multiple taxes and levies; inadequate market information; perishability of some NTFPs; too many middlemen
questions.explanation: Marketing moves forest products from forest to consumer. Agencies include timber contractors, sawmillers, forestry departments, co-operatives, wholesalers and exporters. They assemble, transport, store, process, grade, finance, inform and distribute. Problems include poor roads, bulky products, poor storage, price instability, illegal logging and multiple levies.

questions.stem:
(a) What are non-timber forest products (NTFPs)? [2 marks]
(b) Name six NTFPs harvested in Nigeria and state one use of each. [12 marks]
(c) State three sustainable practices to be observed when harvesting NTFPs and three benefits of NTFPs to rural households. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Products other than timber obtained from forests, such as fruits, nuts, leaves, barks, resins, honey, mushrooms and animals
12 marks: (b) Any six, 1 mark for product and 1 mark for use: bush mango (ogbono) - soup thickener; chewing sticks - oral hygiene; honey - food/medicine; afang (Gnetum) leaves - vegetable; snails - meat/protein; rattan/cane - furniture, baskets; gum arabic - food industry/adhesive; locust bean - condiment (iru/dawadawa); shea nuts - shea butter; medicinal barks/roots - herbal medicine; kola nuts - stimulant; mushrooms - food; raffia - mats, palm wine
3 marks: (c) Sustainable practices, any three: harvest only mature products; avoid destroying the whole plant (e.g. do not fell trees to collect fruits); leave some for regeneration/wildlife; harvest bark in strips without girdling; observe closed seasons; replant/domesticate useful species
3 marks: (c) Benefits, any three: income/employment; food and nutrition; medicine; materials for crafts and building; fuel; cultural uses
questions.explanation: NTFPs are forest products other than timber. Examples include ogbono (soup), chewing sticks, honey, afang leaves, snails, rattan, gum arabic, locust bean, shea nuts and medicinal plants. Sustainable harvesting takes only mature products without destroying plants and leaves some for regeneration. NTFPs provide income, food, medicine and craft materials.
